chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Jazz history ignored: why older bands are not played
summary: Ted Jr. contrasts the Boston Symphony's range with jazz bands that never play Moten or Henderson, and describes his college history course being dismissed.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I'd just like to ask a question for anybody. First of all, today, I had one of the pleasures of my life. I saw my favorite orchestra, the Boston Symphony, playing in its own hall, which was just magnificent. Now they did a program that consisted of work by Michael Colgrass, a composer I know, that was done in 1977. Then they did one of

Haydn the Paris symphonies, which was from the 1780's, and they did something from the 1880's. Now that's quite a span, quite a spectrum of musical styles -- and all of them were done with extraordinary excellence. The orchestra was great, the conductor was great and so forth.

I notice that in jazz, like for instance, you commented to Steven that Coltrane is his era -- you hear these bands like in North State Texas and so forth, all of them playing very well, doing the compositions of Thayer Jones, and all the people, with the Maynard Ferguson sound and the like -- but you never hear anybody play anything like Ben Moten or Fletcher Henderson, like Jay McShann, by anybody, or even the lesser known bands further back. And I find that you see, when the rock era came in, all this sort of disappeared, but I remember back in the fifties, the war between the musicians of the older generation; say, of your generation -- and the newer ones, and they're saying well, that was okay then, but we have to move forward now.

And in the classical world, they've never said you're moving forward because the other is inferior. You add to it, but you keep it all together and the great masters of Europe that go all the way back to Michael Praetorius, even back to the Gregorian period, are still preserved to this day, but yet, very few people know of Benny Moten or Eddie Durham, and any of these people --
That should be taught at Berklee

But you see, that was what I was teaching at Kings borough Community College, and as I said, it didn't make a difference to the department; as a matter of fact, they thought I was just burdening the curriculum, and they said who needs all that old stuff?

And yet, they will put all that emphasis on Gregorian chant and -- but I maintain if you're going to keep American music, the whole history of American music, the only thing around today is built on those earlier bands.

You can get some really exciting music. But this stuff now, as brilliant as it is, a lot of brilliant music-- these people who started with Coltrane--it's do impossible things -- but it's sterile; it's got no body to it. A lot of that music, you hear from all those guys taking all these courses and running up and down the horns the way they do -- it's like an egg that's been punctured and there's no inside to it, just like a shell.
Well, that's what they preserve, and not the really golden stuff of like your generation or even before, like your bands and so forth.
